chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
title: Jimmy Harrison's swing trombone and those who copied him
summary: Jackson calls Harrison the greatest swing trombonist he heard, with Sandy Williams and Jack Teagarden borrowing from him.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: -- he and Claude Jones. Jimmy Harrison at that time was the greatest swing trombone player that I ever heard. He could do more with five notes. He could play five notes and use them so they would swing you to death and then still be interesting, you see.
And a lot of trombone players stole his style, you know. I tell you who sounded closest to him, of the trombone players almost of today, I'll say. Sandy Williams played like him.

Teagarden stole a lot of things from him. I have to say stole because that's the truth. You know, Teagarden used to come up in Fletcher's band and want to sit in with him and play, you know, just like Benny Goodman used to come up and want to sit in Fletcher's band up in Harlem when he came to town when they was with Ben Pollack, you see.
: That's amazing how some of those stories -- I've heard this so many times before -- how those stories all coincide, --
: -- [and you] reaffirm the truthfulness of it.
